Notable but less significant changes to the approach taken for Element 1 in the 2025 WWAP versus the 2015 WWAP are summarized below.

The nonbreeding rank has been removed. State ranks were assessed for bird species that nested in Wisconsin in at least three of the last five years. To simplify and standardize the ranking process, the resul�ng ranks are thus for nes�ng species and, importantly, reflect only the species' breeding status.

div.head: Mammal SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGCN
div.p: Mammals play an important role in ecosystem function as top of the food-chain predators, and likewise, serving as prey for numerous other predators. Mammals provide an important means of disturbance for plant communities and by indirect influence, the size and composition of many insect communities, as well. There are 71 native mammal species in Wisconsin. Eighteen were reviewed and assessed by the Mammal Taxon Team using the rank calculator and 53 without, and 11 (15%) were identified as SGCN and 10 (14%) were identified as SGIN (Table E1.3). Six are listed as Threatened or Endangered at the state or federal level.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of mammal SGCN can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 16 A comprehensive table with SGCN/SGIN results for all animal and plant groups, including summarized notes, can be found in the 2025 WWAP collection for Element 1.foot_11 A summary of changes between the 2015 and 2025 WWAP for all species is provided in Table E1.13 at the end of this section. In addition to the NHI database and expert knowledge, a wide variety of resources were used during the assessment process, including information from the Midwest Bat Working Group (MWBWG) and recent small mammal monitoring efforts. These and other data informed the process to help determine which species should be or remain SGCN, SGIN, or removed from the list altogether. Some species like American Water Shrew (Sorex palustris) were moved from SGCN to SGIN due to vulnerability in Wisconsin and the need for more survey effort. Others, such as Little Brown Bat (Myotis lucifigus), remained SGCN due to the many threats and large population declines.

Although all taxonomic groups used the same process to identify Wisconsin's SGCN, bat species face an uncertain future from the long-term threat of White-nose Syndrome (WNS In relation to assessing small mammals for SGCN, a 2014 publication by Stephens and Anderson shed much light on the habitat associations and assemblages of small mammals throughout the state in numerous plant communities. These data were tremendously helpful in assessing the status of many small mammals and reinforced the rarity of many of those found on the initial SGCN list (WDNR 2005) that remain on the list in 2025. There is still a paucity of information for several of our small mammal species due to their cryptic nature, lack of effective and reliable detection methods, and/or simply low population numbers.

Of the state's remaining native mammal species, some are very common or stable and relatively speaking are not in need of conservation (e.g., raccoon, striped skunk) or they may be managed as game species (e.g., deer). These mammals were not assessed for SGCN status. For some mammal species an assessment was deemed "not applicable" (NatureServe Rank = SNA) because the species is not a suitable target for conservation activities. A species can be "not applicable" for several reasons: their presence here is unpredictable or infrequent, there are no permanent breeding pairs, there isn't a sustainable population, or we can't identify a habitat or territory that it uses. These species include cougar, Canada lynx and Indiana bat. In our state, these species bring important issues to the forefront about what defines a native species and the circumstances that qualify a species for conservation need, especially with species and habitat shifts occurring because of climate and other environmental changes.

div.head: References for Mammal Species of Greatest Conservation Need
div.p: Information sources used in the evaluation and assessment of mammal species SGCN/SGIN are described in Appendix E1, Item 4 Species Information Sources. Some information about rare species locations is confidential or comes to us through informal technical reports or memos.

For these various reasons, we also relied significantly on expert and professional observations and unpublished data. Species experts assessed each species' rarity, threats and trends according to the NatureServe Conservation Status Assessment Methodology. Vulnerability to environmental change, status in Wisconsin and genetic diversity were also assessed. Species were then each assigned an Srankfoot_13 following NatureServe's Natural Heritage Methodology and those with an S-rank of S1 or S2, and some species with an S-rank of S3 or any combination thereof (e.g., S1S2, S2S3) became SGCN. Species that do not have sufficient information to be ranked or do not meet the criteria for SGCN but are of concern to experts become Species of Information Need (SGIN): SGINranking or SGIN-monitoring, respectively. Other species had sufficient information to assess their SGCN status, and did not meet the SGCN criteria; however, information may still be gathered to monitor their populations and habitat in the event their status changes. Details on the process of identifying SGCN and SGIN can be found above in E1.2 Methods.

Beginning in 2023, state ranks were assessed for bird species that nested in Wisconsin in at least three of the last five years; the resulting ranks reflect only Wisconsin's nesting species, and importantly, on the species' breeding status in the state. Although we acknowledge the migratory nature of many birds, non-breeding statusfoot_14 is no longer used to simplify and standardize the ranking process, although the full annual life cycle was considered during the rank assessment process. Efforts to address species' conservation needs during migration and winter remain important. For some non-breeding species, their habitat and conservation requirements can be met through ranked breeding birds, while others, like shorebirds, are incorporated by proxy through the plan's threats and actions that are outside the context of ranking or SGCN/SGIN designation.

div.head: Bird SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGCN
div.p: Birds play an important role in ecosystem function and a wide array of roles in the habitats in which they occur. Wisconsin provides important breeding, wintering, or migratory habitat for approximately 284 native bird species, which includes 225 breeding birds and another 50+ migrant/wintering species. 21 Of the 284 species, 165 were reviewed and assessed by the Bird Taxon Team without the calculator and 65 with the rank calculator. From this, 49 (17%) of native bird species were identified as SGCN and 22 (8%) were identified as SGIN (Table E1.4). Twenty-two are currently listed as Threatened or Endangered in Wisconsin; one is listed as federally Threatened or Endangered, and one is listed federally as an Experimental, Non-Essential Population.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of bird SGCNs can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 22 A comprehensive table with SGCN/SGIN results for all animal and plant groups, including summarized notes, can be found in the 2025 WWAP collection for Element 1.foot_17 A summary of changes between the 2015 and 2025 WWAP for all species is provided in Table E1.13 at the end of this section.

The DNR's Breeding Bird Atlas IIfoot_18 , which ran from 2015-2019, helped document the distribution and abundance of breeding birds in the state and significantly improved our understanding of their population changes in light of the numerous threats they face, including climate change and loss of habitat. Along with other resources, the atlas helped inform the assessment process in determining which species should be or remain SGCN, SGIN, or removed from the list altogether. Some species like American Woodcock were removed from the SGCN list due to a population increase. Others, such as Dark-eyed Junco, were added as SGIN due to declining trends and vulnerability to climate change and to highlight future monitoring needs.

Of our state's remaining native bird species, some are very common or stable and, relatively speaking, are not in need of conservation (e.g., blue jay and American crow) and some of those may be managed as game species (e.g., mourning dove and wild turkey). For some bird species an assessment was considered not applicable (rank = SNA) because the species is not a suitable target for conservation activities. A species can be "not applicable" for a couple reasons: their presence here is unpredictable or infrequent, there are no permanent breeding pairs, there isn't a sustainable population, or we can't identify a habitat or territory that it uses. These species include long distance migrants such as the marbled godwit, and species that do not regularly breed within the state such as the barn owl and snowy egret. In our state, these species bring important issues to the forefront about what defines a native species and the circumstances that qualify a species for conservation need, especially with species and habitat shifts occurring as a result of climate and other environmental changes.

div.head: Fish SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGCN
div.p: There are 148 native fish species in Wisconsin. Of these, 40 were reviewed and 23 (16%) were identified as SSGCN and 7 (18%) were identified as SGIN in Wisconsin. Twenty are listed as Threatened or Endangered in Wisconsin and two are Special Concern. Fish SGCN and SGIN are listed in Table E1.5.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of fish SGCN can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 27 A comprehensive table with SGCN/SGIN results for all animal and plant groups, including summarized notes, can be found in the 2025 WWAP collection for Element 1. 28 Many of our fish Species of Greatest Conservation Need are found only in large river systems such as the Mississippi and Wisconsin rivers, which have been highly altered with dams and other hydraulic control infrastructure. Restoration of the natural processes that characterize these systems would help conserve many of these species by providing the natural flow regime, connectivity and specific habitats that these large river species need throughout their life cycles. Most fish SGCN are warm water habitat species that coincide with areas of the state where development and use of aquatic resources and adjacent lands is greatest, which underscores the need and opportunity for collaborative conservation.

Of our states remaining, non-SGCN or SGIN native fish species, some are common or stable and presently are not in need of conservation (e.g., rainbow darter, southern redbelly dace, tadpole madtom) or they are managed as species that are fished (e.g., brook trout, walleye, smallmouth bass). These fish species were not assessed for SGCN status. Presently there are no fish species ranked as SNA or "not applicable" because they are an unsuitable target for conservation activities or their presence here is unpredictable or infrequent. However, changes and extreme fluctuations in water temperature, quality and quantity as well as competition for surface and ground water resources may result in changes abundance and distribution (i.e., the status of a species).

div.head: Herptile SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGIN
div.p: Herptiles use a wide variety of habitats from sand prairies to streams to ephemeral ponds. Many herptile SGCN are distinguished by their use of a combination of terrestrial, wetland and aquatic habitats to meet their life history and ecological needs. As a group, this makes them vulnerable to threats from sources acting in multiple environments. There are 55 native herptile 32 species in Wisconsin, which includes 36 reptiles and 19 amphibians. In all, 38 species were reviewed and assessed without the calculator and 20 with the rank calculator. This included 3 historical species no longer considered present. As a result, 25 (45%) were identified as SGCN and four as SGIN (Table 1.4). Eight are currently listed as Threatened or Endangered in Wisconsin.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of amphibian and reptile SGCN can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 33 animal and plant groups, including summarized notes, can be found in the 2025 WWAP collection for Element 1.foot_25

In addition to the NHI database and expert knowledge, a wide variety of resources were used during the assessment process, including the Wisconsin Frog and Toad Survey a citizen-based monitoring program that began in 1981 to assess status, distribution and long-term population trends of Wisconsin's twelve frog and toad species. These and other data helped herp experts determine which species should be or remain SGCN, SGIN, or removed from the list altogether. Some species like the Common Five-lined Skink (Plestiodon fasciatus) are widespread but were added as SGIN to highlight the need for more information in light of the many threats it currently faces. Whereas the northern leopard frog (Lithobates pipiens) was removed as SGIN as the species is apparently now secure and no longer in need of close monitoring.

div.head: Invertebrate Animal SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGCN
div.p: Invertebrate animals make up 94% of the world's animal species. There are estimated to be over 25,000 native invertebrate species in Wisconsin. Of these 1048 (4%) were assessed and 335 (1.3%) have been identified as SGCN and SGIN in Wisconsin (Table E1.9). Forty-four are currently listed as Threatened or Endangered in Wisconsin. Nine are federally endangered, three are federal Species of Concern, two are proposed for federal listing and one is a candidate for listing.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of invertebrate SGCN can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 38 The Wisconsin Bumble Bee Brigade (DNR), Wisconsin Odonata Survey (DNR and Wisconsin Dragonfly Society) and Wisconsin Mussel Monitoring (DNR) projects, along with crowd-sourced observation platforms such as iNaturalist and BugGuide, helped document the distribution and abundance of many invertebrate groups in the state and significantly improved our understanding of their population changes in light of the numerous threats they face, including climate change and loss of habitat. Along with other resources and via expert input, these monitoring projects provided critical data needed to determine which species should be SGCN, SGIN, or removed from the list altogether. Some species like Yellow Bumble Bee were removed from the SGCN list due to its wide range and occupancy in the state. Others, such as Northern Clearwater Crayfish, were added as SGIN due to declining trends regionally and vulnerability to climate change and to highlight future monitoring needs.

Other groups such as grasshoppers, beetles, snails, spiders, crustaceans, mayflies, stoneflies, specialist bees, caddisflies and true bugs lack statewide survey effort and do not have aggregated datasets needed to quantify range and abundance in the state. Instead, we relied heavily upon input by experts to identify species with narrow habitat specificity and species sensitive to degraded habitat quality. Many 2015 SGCNs from these groups were added to the 2025 SGIN list when research and inventory were identified as the primary conservation need. Additionally, there are many groups for which we cannot even compile a Wisconsin species list much less describe which species are of conservation need. The lack of information has fostered extensive public misunderstanding regarding many invertebrate species. Wisconsin is not alone; most invertebrate groups have not been studied or catalogued and basic lists of species are lacking for most taxa in most states.

Of our state's remaining native invertebrate species, some are very common or stable and, relatively speaking, are not in need of conservation (e.g., Common Green Darner dragonfly and Painted Lady butterfly). For some invertebrate species an assessment was considered not applicable (rank = SNA) because the species is not a suitable target for conservation activities. A species can be "not applicable" for a couple reasons: their presence here is unpredictable or infrequent, their presence has not been confirmed and they are not considered native. These species include facultative migrants such as the Painted Skimmer and Comet Darner dragonflies, and species that do not regularly occur within the state such as the Southern Cloudy Wing butterfly. In our state, these species bring important issues to the forefront about what defines a native species and the circumstances that qualify a species for conservation need, especially with species and habitat shifts occurring as a result of climate and other environmental changes.

div.head: SGCN, SGIN, and other species not SGCN
div.p: The Wisconsin WAP stresses the importance of protecting habitats as a means of protecting entire suites of species, which is why plant SGCNs have been incorporated into this plan. The first plan (2005) stated that protecting "rare plants" was a management opportunity for some natural communities or ecological landscapes. However, by specifically identifying and describing plant SGCNs in the same way as animal SGCNs (i.e., with association scores, threats and actions, and Conservation Opportunity Areas), users can make more complete and comprehensive decisions about conservation actions, their targets and where to implement them on the landscape, giving the plan greater value as a centralized, go-to source for conservation priorities and options that incorporate complete ecosystems.

There are roughly 2,640 45 native vascular plants (including hybrids and infraspecific taxa) in Wisconsin, which is similar to other states in the Upper Great Lakes region. Of these, 318 vascular plant species were reviewed and assessed by the Plant Taxon Team without the rank calculator and 69 with the calculator. Another 194 bryophytes and lichens were also reviewed without the rank calculator. Of the native vascular species, 295 (11%) were identified as Species of Greatest Conservation Need and 26 as SGIN (Table E1.10). A total of 130 native vascular plants are listed as state threatened or endangered, 192 as special concern and six plants are listed as federally threatened. For bryophytes, 105 were reviewed with 59 identified as SGCN and 21 as SGIN. Similarly, 105 lichens were reviewed with 85 identified as SGCN and 9 as SGIN.

Information about the status, distribution and biology of vascular plant (i.e., mosses and lichens are not included) SGCN can be found on the NHI biodiversity pages. 46 A comprehensive table with SGCN/SGIN results for all animal and plant groups, including summarized notes, can be found in the 2025 WWAP collection for Element 1.foot_34 A summary of changes between the 2015 and 2025 WWAP for all species is provided in Table E1.11 at the end of this section.

Rare plant habitats can vary greatly in size and quality, with species occurring in both large blocks of high-quality undisturbed habitats as well as small, remnant, isolated sites. The plant team recognized that unknown trends or uncertain threat impacts to plants were a common challenge to defining SGCNs.

Of our states remaining native plant species, some are common or stable and relatively speaking are not in need of conservation (e.g., sugar maple, sweet cicely, blue-joint grass, etc.). These plant species were not assessed for SGCN status. Environmental changes and the fact that many rare species persist as unknown remnant populations, will necessitate periodic reassessment of how plant species are distributed among these categories (i.e., common/stable, assessed but not SGCN or SGIN).
